10294-verse-and-prose-for-beginners-in-r:
This 1893 school reader gathers verse and prose for pupils just leaving a primer behind. Its editors drew on English and American literature, choosing pieces short enough for young readers to master with care. Verse fills most of the book, while prose appears mainly as proverbs and familiar sayings.

The preface explains that a primer can only lead a child toward literature, not give it in full. This book takes the next step, with poems, sayings, and brief prose that build taste and skill. Readers get a gentle, period introduction to English verse, made for classroom use.
1047-the-new-machiavelli:
H. G. Wells tells of Richard Remington, a bright young man who rises from Cambridge to Parliament as a reforming socialist, then wrecks his career for love. The novel mixes politics, journalism, and private passion, and it draws on Wells's own years among the Fabians and the press.

Remington's wife, his mistress, and his party each pull him a different way, and his grand schemes for a new England founder on human weakness. Wells uses the tale to argue for able, honest rule and to mock party cant. The book is long and frank, and it gives a vivid picture of Edwardian political life.
10870-are-you-a-bromide-the-sulphitic-th:
Gelett Burgess, author of the Goops books, published Are You a Bromide? in 1906, expounding his sulphitic theory of boredom. The essay, revised from the Smart Set of April 1906, divides people into Bromides, who repeat dull, conventional phrases, and Sulphites, who think and speak for themselves. Well-known "bromidioms" now in use illustrate the types.

Burgess decorates the book himself and dedicates it to Gertrude McCall, discoverer of the theory. His humor is light but pointed, aimed at dinner-table dullness. Readers get a witty piece of Edwardian psychology, and a word, bromide, that entered the language from it.
19814-three-years-in-france-with-the-gun:
Three Years in France with the Guns gives episodes in the life of a British artillery officer. One scene finds a subaltern waking from deep slumber in a train carriage. He peers out and groans at the beastly hole of Bouvette. His surprise at the laughter around him follows. The book's voice is dry, tired, and amused. It is the Western Front remembered by a gunner.

Artillery war was noise, mud, and long waiting between shoots. Officers' memoirs from the batteries are rarer than infantry ones. Episodes, rather than a grand narrative, suit that disjointed war. Humor carries scenes that horror would flatten. Readers get the guns' war at human scale. Such memoirs grounded Britain's memory of France.
19927-the-continental-monthly-vol-2-no-2:
The Continental Monthly for August 1862 is volume 2, number 2 of a wartime magazine. It declares itself devoted to literature and national policy. One story scene stands by a little run, four hundred yards from a farmhouse. A turpentine distillery occupies the bank there. Rosin and turpentine works scatter around it. Fiction, poetry, and war argument shared such numbers.

New York published the Continental through the Civil War's middle years. It mixed Southern scenes with Union politics deliberately. Turpentine country meant the pine barrens of the Carolinas. Stories grounded national policy in local color. A single issue shows the magazine's whole method. It remains useful to students of wartime print.
20565-the-continental-monthly-vol-6-no-2:
The Continental Monthly for August 1864, volume 6, number 2, mixes literature with the politics of a nation at war. The magazine spoke for the Union cause. Its essays scold the loose language of wartime debate as much as they praise the cause.

One writer complains that words like fool and tyrant are thrown at men the people have delighted to honor. Such language disgusts older and more thoughtful readers. It has become, he says, a recognized fact of the time. The issue shows how the Civil War filled even literary monthlies with argument about the nation's words and deeds.
22062-the-mathematicall-praeface-to-elem:
John Dee, Elizabeth I's famous astrologer-philosopher, wrote the Mathematicall Praeface for the first English Euclid in 1570. Henry Billingsley had translated the Elements of Geometrie; Dee's preface introduces it. He calls the preface very fruitful, specifying the chief mathematical sciences, what they are, and what they are good for. He also promises to disclose certain new mathematical and mechanical secrets, much missed until these days.

Dee maps arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, optics, music, and dozens of lesser arts in one great tree. He defends mathematics against charges of conjuring. The Praeface is a landmark of English science writing, and it made Dee's name across Europe. Readers still meet it as the gateway to Tudor mathematics.
22150-the-theories-of-darwin-and-their-r:
Eduard von Hartmann, the German philosopher, examined Darwin's theories and their bearing on philosophy, religion, and morals. His book, translated for English readers, addresses a troubled audience. Hartmann writes for people who feel they must set themselves right on these questions. They touch mankind's highest interests, yet few lay readers have time to master the sciences involved.

Hartmann argues that evolution and purpose need not be enemies. He defends a philosophy in which nature's process has meaning beyond blind chance. Religious and ethical views, he notes, remained sharply opposed after Darwin. The book is a period piece from the first great age of Darwin debates, when every thinker had to reckon with the new biology.
22690-rembrandt-and-his-works-comprising:
John Burnet wrote Rembrandt and His Works, a short account of the Dutch master's life and art, illustrated with examples from his etchings. The catalog record gives no year. Burnet, himself a painter and engraver, wrote for readers who admired Rembrandt but lacked access to the prints and paintings scattered across Europe.

In the preface, Burnet notes the limits set on the book's size and plates, while doing his publisher justice for sparing no expense to credit the great artist. Preparing the work showed him how wide the interest ran in making Rembrandt better appreciated. The text mixes biography with close looks at single etchings. It stands as an early English attempt to bring Rembrandt to a broad public, and it still reads with a practitioner's respect.
3381-the-standard-household-effect-compa:
William Dean Howells makes a household joke out of spring cleaning in this short essay from Literature and Life. A visitor reports that every rug in his house has been up for weeks, while furniture sits wrapped and the family lives on bare floors. Howells calls the force behind this yearly upheaval the eternal womanly, a teasing name for the drive to scour a home from top to bottom.

The essay argues, with a straight face, that modern comforts have made housekeeping harder rather than easier. Each new rug, curtain, and pretty object adds one more thing to dust, guard against moths, and keep clean. Grandmothers had fewer goods to tend, Howells says, and so carried a lighter load. Readers get a witty look at late Victorian domestic life and at how progress can quietly add work.
4655-the-seigneurs-of-old-canada-a-chron:
William Bennett Munro wrote The Seigneurs of Old Canada as volume five of the Chronicles of Canada, edited by George M. Wrong and H. H. Langton, and published at Toronto in 1915. Its subtitle names its theme: a chronicle of New-World feudalism. Munro opens by asking what history would be without the picturesque annals of the Gallic race, whose prestige and power shaped European politics from Charlemagne to the last Bonaparte.

From that wide view he turns to New France, where seigneurs held land, tenants owed dues, and French custom met a hard northern land. The book explains how feudal forms took root in Canada, and how they bent under war, trade, and settlement. Readers get a clear, short history of French Canada's land system, useful for understanding Quebec's past, and for seeing feudalism far from its European home.
4988-the-outdoor-girls-at-wild-rose-lodg:
Laura Lee Hope's Outdoor Girls at Wild Rose Lodge sends Betty and her friends toward a lodge holiday. Falling trees, a queer little man, good news, and a dare Betty takes fill the early chapters. Bad tidings are confirmed. Premonitions follow. A visitor arrives. A hold-up raises the stakes, while Allen earns cheers and the enemy is routed.

Wild roses, a whirlpool, a moonlight apparition, and a tragedy keep the mystery strand taut, until the old crowd gathers again and what seemed lost is recovered. Hope keeps the friendships warm through every scare. Readers get a girls' camp adventure with a hermit, a haunting, and plenty of outdoor fun.
6380-cornelli:
Johanna Spyri, known too narrowly for Heidi, writes Cornelli as a second Swiss child's tale, says the foreword, for writers suffer injustice in being known by one book alone. Spring comes again on the banks of the Iller stream. Beech trees sway, clouds drive across the sun, and a little girl with glowing cheeks and blowing hair runs through the wood, hat dangling from fluttering ribbons. She sings of snow on meadows, cuckoo, flowers, and kindliest sun.

Cornelli, obstinate and warm, throws a thing down on purpose and tells Miss Mina she does not care, then walks happily next morning hand in hand with her teacher, Mr. Malinger, kind as ever. School hours wash away yesterday's troubles, and the child who sang in the wind learns steadiness. Spyri writes a gentle story of temper, teachers, and spring, where a Swiss girl grows by small, daily kindnesses.
7175-the-tattva-muktavali:
Purnananda Chakravartin, a native of Bengal, wrote the Tattva-muktavali as a poem whose date no one can fix with certainty. E. B. Cowell edited and translated it for the Royal Asiatic Society journal in 1883. If it were the same poem Madhava names in his account of Ramanuja, it would predate the fourteenth century. Cowell himself leans to a later date.

That doubt becomes part of the poem's interest, since its ideas must be read without a firm place in time. The translation presents the text as a work of Indian thought in verse, preserved through learned journals rather than through wide fame. Readers meet a voice from Bengal speaking in the measured form of a philosophical poem.
8211-the-outdoor-girls-at-wild-rose-lodg:
Laura Lee Hope, author of The Outdoor Girls of Deepdale, The Bobbsey Twins, and many other series, wrote this Outdoor Girls adventure at Wild Rose Lodge, subtitled The Hermit of Moonlight Falls. Its chapters promise fun, a falling tree, a queer little man, Betty taking a dare, a near wreck, a hold-up. Sheep, an enemy routed, wild roses, a whirlpool, and a mysterious thing that proves very much alive. The girls' holiday turns into a mystery around the hermit.

The novel follows the series pattern: friendship, outdoor adventure, and a puzzle solved by plucky heroines. Its lodge setting gives it summer-camp charm. For young readers and collectors of girls' series fiction, it is a cheerful example of the genre, and a nostalgic visit to an era of wholesome adventure.
9075-rico-and-wiseli:
Johanna Spyri, famed for Heidi, wrote these two Swiss tales, here translated by Louise Brooks. Rico and Stineli follows a boy on the Lake of Sils, with an old schoolmaster's fiddle, a lake without a name, and a precious legacy left by his mother. How Wiseli Was Provided For tells of an orphan girl found a home.

Both tales prize kindness, faith, and the beauty of mountain lakes and villages. Spyri writes simply, for children and their elders alike. The pair still delights as gentle Alpine stories of loss, friendship, and care.
9963-elsie-s-girlhood-a-sequel-to-elsie-:
Martha Finley's 1872 novel continues the story of Elsie Dinsmore, now growing from child to young woman. It opens at a fashionable watering place, where Elsie, her father Mr. Dinsmore, and Rose and Edward Allison keep comfortable hotel rooms and a private parlor.

The sequel follows Elsie's girlhood with the gentle moral tone of the earlier books: trust, love, and happy innocence, tested by the wider world. Finley's readers, mostly girls, found a heroine whose faith guided her friendships and choices. The book remains a clear example of nineteenth-century domestic fiction for young readers.
amenities-of-literature-consisting-of-sk:
Amenities of Literature, by Isaac Disraeli, collects sketches and characters of English literature. Disraeli, who wrote as Isaac D'Israeli and was the father of the prime minister, published the book in 1841 at the age of seventy-five; this edition dates from 1871. He meant it as a companion to his earlier Curiosities of Literature and Miscellanies of Literature.

The book was planned as part of a much larger work, a history of vernacular literature, that he never completed. What stands instead is a set of literary portraits and essays, written for pleasure by a lifelong man of letters. Readers get the elder Disraeli's hobby in bound form: anecdotal, curious criticism that preserves how the nineteenth century enjoyed its own literary past.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acciajuoli:
Acciajuoli is the name of three cardinals from an illustrious Florentine family. Angelo, born in 1349 and dead at Pisa in 1408, was noted for learning, experience, and integrity. Urban VI made him Florence's archbishop in 1383 and cardinal in 1385, he resisted every effort to draw him to the antipope Clement VII. He defended Urban's election by word and deed.

After Urban's death, half the conclave's votes went to Acciajuoli, but he steered the election toward Boniface IX to end the schism. Boniface named him Ostia's cardinal-bishop, dispatching him to Germany, Slavonia, and Bulgaria. Niccolo, born in 1630, died at Rome in 1719 as Cardinal-Bishop of Ostia. Filippo, nuncio in Portugal, was expelled by Pombal in 1760 for backing the Jesuits and died at Ancona in 1766.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acephali:
Acephali, headless ones, is the term for Eutychians who withdrew from Peter Mongus, Monophysite head of Alexandria, in 482. Peter Mongus and Acacius of Constantinople had framed a new creed against Nestorius and Eutyches expressly, while passing over the Council of Chalcedon and rejecting it in bad faith. Emperor Zeno approved this vague formula and imposed it in his Henoticon, or edict of union.

The condemnation of Eutyches angered rigid Monophysites, and the unclear stance toward Chalcedon seemed insufficient. Many, especially monks, left Peter Mongus, choosing no head over staying in communion with him. Later they sided with Severus, Monophysite head of Antioch. Deacon Liberatus instead traces the name to Ephesus, to those following neither Alexandria's Cyril nor Antioch's John.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-advocatus-dia:
Advocatus Diaboli, Advocate of the Devil or Devil's Advocate, is the popular title of a leading officer of the Sacred Congregation of Rites. Sixtus V set up that body in 1587 to handle beatification and canonization cases. Promoter of the Faith, Promotor Fidei, is his official title; his duty is preparing in writing all possible arguments against raising anyone to the honours of the altar.

The church's interest and honour demand that no one receive honours whose death is not juridically proved precious in God's sight. Prospero Lambertini, later Benedict XIV, served twenty years as Promoter of the Faith and wrote his great work on beatification and canonization from that experience. No important act in the process counts unless done in the Promoter's formal presence. Urban VIII in 1631 made his presence, at least by deputy, necessary for validity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alfonso-muzza:
Alfonso Muzzarelli was an Italian Jesuit, born at Ferrara in 1749 and dead at Paris in 1813. He joined the Jesuits in 1768, then taught at Bologna and Imola. After the order's suppression in 1773 he took a Ferrara benefice, then directed Parma's College of Nobles. Pius VII called him to Rome as Penitentiary theologian.

Exiled with Pius VII in 1809, Muzzarelli left Rome for Paris, where he spent his remaining years at a Paris convent. He wrote numerous theological and ascetical works. His chief production, The Good Use of Logic in Matters of Religion, gathers philosophico-theological treatises. It appeared in six volumes at Foligno in 1787 to 1789, ten at Rome in 1807, and eleven at Florence in 1821. It treats abuses in the Church, the pope's temporal power, toleration, indulgences, confession, and moral liberty. He also refuted Rousseau's Emile and Social Contract, and his Month of Mary reached about a hundred editions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aloysius-gent:
Aloysius Gentili was born at Rome in 1801 and died at Dublin in 1848. A poet and musician, mechanically and electrically inclined, devoted to languages, he lived as a brilliant young man of the world. Ambitious nobly, he was society's pet, fortune's favourite. He sought Jesuit admission, but his health prevented acceptance. Remaining in Rome, he attended lectures at the Irish College to improve his English, ordained in 1830, then made his novitiate at Domodossola.

At the Irish College, the convert Ambrose Phillips de Lisle asked for a priest to preach in England. Gentili served two years as Prior Park president, but Baines's mixing of secular and regular professors ended with the fathers' withdrawal. The first public mission at Loughborough, by Gentili and Furlong, succeeded, with sixty-three converts instructed and received. From 1844 to 1848 missions and retreats across England filled his years. At Newcastle 250 adult Protestants were received; three Manchester missions produced 378 converts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aloysius-tapa:
Aloysius Taparelli, christened Prospero of the D'Azeglio family, was a philosopher and sociological writer, born at Turin in 1793, dead at Rome in 1862, buried near St. Aloysius's altar in St. Ignatius's. His father Cesare was Sardinian ambassador to the Holy See; his brother Massimo, an Italian minister of state. Educated by the Calasanctians at Siena and Turin's Atheneo, he attended St-Cyr for some months but soldiering was not his destiny. He entered the Jesuits at Rome in 1814.

In youth he showed a bent for mechanics, painting, music. He later invented the violicembolo, praised by Liszt, renamed the symphonium at his suggestion. He was first rector of the Roman College after its restoration to the Jesuits. He taught philosophy sixteen years at Palermo, then joined Civiltà Cattolica. His chief work, A Theoretical Essay on Natural Right, began modern sociology in a way. It was translated into German.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-angelo-claren:
Angelo Clareno da Cingoli, Spiritual Franciscan leader, was born at Fossombrone about 1247 and died at Santa Maria d'Aspro in 1337. He entered the order in 1262 or thereabouts. Believing Saint Francis's rule was not observed as intended, he retired to a hermitage with companions and formed the Clareni.

By Sixtus IV's Bull, the Clareni were united to the main order under the Minister General. Joachim of Floris's prophecies influenced Angelo, who awaited restored discipline under a papa angelicus and a new order of Friars. But his followers were few, and his extreme reading of Saint Francis's rule drew the Friars Minor's disfavour. He wandered homeless through Greece, Armenia, and Italy until, in 1311, he came to Avignon to answer a heresy charge and was acquitted. In 1337 he retired to Santa Maria d'Aspro, where he died in the odour of sanctity on 15 June. He authored, at least in part, the Chronica septem tribulationum.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-raval:
Italian Jesuit missionary Antonio Ravalli, born in 1811 and dead at St. Mary's, Montana, in 1884, answered Father de Smet's call for the American mission in 1843. He sailed with priests, a brother, and six sisters of Notre Dame de Namur, reaching Fort Vancouver in August 1844 after eight months at sea. After a short stay at St. Paul on the Willamette in Oregon, where he studied English and tended the sick, he joined Father Hoeck in spring 1845 at St. Ignatius among the Kalispel, or Pend d'Oreille, people.

Later he took charge of the Flathead mission of St. Mary's along the Bitter Root River in western Montana, then, after its temporary abandonment, of the Sacred Heart mission among the Coeur d'Alenes in northern Idaho from 1854. There he designed and built a handsome church, carving its altar and statues himself. Governor Stevens praised Ravalli's skill as an architect.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-atto-of-verce:
Atto of Vercelli was a learned theologian and canonist, a scholar of church law, in tenth-century Italy. Son of Viscount Aldegarius, he held the bishopric of Vercelli from 924 to 961. In 933 he became grand chancellor to King Lothaire II, winning gifts and privileges for his see. He is sometimes called Atto II, to set him apart from an earlier bishop of Vercelli with the same name.

His writings reached print in stages, from D'Achery's seventeenth-century selections to a full two-volume edition in 1768, including his long commentary on St Paul's letters. His Canones gathered church legislation, including the false Decretals, alongside his own rules, and they remain valuable for northern Italian church life of the time. Cardinal Mai later published his sermons and his puzzling Polypticum, a short moral philosophy whose authorship scholars still dispute.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ausculta-fili:
Ausculta Fili, meaning Listen, Son, is a letter sent on 5 December 1301 by Pope Boniface VIII to Philip the Fair, King of France. King and pope were at enmity, and Philip, pleading royal rights, handed out benefices and named bishops to sees without regard for papal authority. He drove from their sees those bishops who stayed loyal to the pope against the king's will. The letter answers that whole quarrel in a single papal voice.

It is written in firm but fatherly terms, setting out the harms the king has brought on his kingdom, on Church, and on State. It invites Philip to do penance and mend his ways. The king paid it no heed, and the letter was followed by the famous bull Unam Sanctam. The entry is short, giving the letter's occasion, temper, and sequel in a few plain sentences.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-autocephali:
Autocephali, from a Greek word for independent, was a name in early Christian times for certain bishops who answered to no patriarch or metropolitan. They answered directly to the triennial provincial synod or to the Apostolic See. Only those tribunals could judge them for heresy or grave offenses. Such were the bishops of Cyprus, of Iberia and Armenia into the age of Photius, of Britain before St Augustine came, and for a while of Ravenna.

The spread of patriarchal authority shrank their number over time. Similar bishops in the patriarchates of Constantinople, Alexandria, and Antioch answered directly to the patriarch of their civil diocese, owing nothing to their local metropolitans. They resembled the modern exempt bishops under Rome. The oldest list of them stands in the ninth-century Notitia of Leo the Wise, where they rank as archbishops and metropolitans without suffragans.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benedetto-cas:
Benedetto Castelli, a Benedictine mathematician and physicist, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Perugia in 1577 and dead at Rome in 1644, he joined the Benedictines at Monte Cassino and rose to abbot. His real passion was mathematics applied to water, the science of moving and measuring rivers and canals.

Galileo taught him, and Torricelli, one of his pupils, joined Galileo in praising his skill and seeking his advice. Pope Urban VIII called him to Rome in 1623, made him chief mathematician to the pope, and gave him a public chair at the university. A mission to study the waters of the Papal States shows his craft in service.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-berenger-fred:
Bérenger Frédoli, cardinal-bishop of Frascati, is the subject of this short 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Vérune in France, he died at Avignon in 1323 after a career that moved from Béziers canonries to a chair of canon law at Bologna. Pope Celestine V made him Bishop of Béziers in 1294.

Boniface VIII set him to help compile the Liber Sextus, a new book of church decrees. He also took a leading part in the pope's hard talks with King Philip the Fair of France. Clement V raised him to cardinal in 1305. The entry sketches a canon lawyer at the centre of the age's great church-state quarrel.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-alexander-: Blessed Alexander Sauli, Apostle of Corsica, was born at Milan in 1533 and died at Pavia in 1592. A Barnabite teacher of philosophy and theology at Pavia, and later superior-general of his congregation, he was made Bishop of Aleria in Corsica in 1571, where faith had nearly died out. With three companions he reclaimed the people, corrected abuses, and restored clergy and schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-conra:
Blessed Conrad of Ascoli, a Franciscan missionary, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Ascoli in 1234 to the noble Milliano family, he died there in 1289. Penance ruled his life from youth, and he entered the Friars Minor with his townsman Girolamo d'Ascoli, later Pope Nicholas IV, studying at Perugia and teaching theology at Rome.

Permission to go to Africa followed. There he preached through Libya with much fruit and many reported miracles. Then came a mission to the King of France and a theology lectureship at Paris. Summoned to Rome in 1288 by his old friend, now pope, who wished him cardinal, he died on the way home at Ascoli. His body, moved in 1371, was found incorrupt and sweet-smelling.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caesar-sporte:
Caesar Sportelli, born at Nola in 1702, was a noted lawyer who joined Saint Alphonsus and became the first clerical novice of his institute. Ordained by his guide Falcoia, later Bishop of Castellamare, he stood by Alphonsus when others left him, and helped more than anyone to spread the institute. He founded the houses of Mater Domini at Caposele and of Pagani, where Alphonsus lived and died.

Sportelli wore himself out in preaching and fell stricken by apoplexy on the road to a retreat. Bandits carried him to Pagani, where he died on 19 April 1750, the day he had foretold. When his coffin was opened three years and seven months later, his body lay whole and fresh while his vestments had turned to dust. His cause was introduced in 1899, when he was declared venerable.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cali:
Cali is a diocese in Colombia, founded on 7 July 1910, covering a province of about 4,175 square miles, rich in gold, sugar, cacao, coffee, and cattle. Cali city, seat of the diocese, holds about 35,000 people and was founded by Captain Miguel Lopez Munoz under Sebastian de Belalcazar on 25 July 1536. An earthquake in 1885 wrecked many of its buildings, but the city recovered fast.

A new railroad to Buenaventura and the Pacific raised its trade, and wide cacao and coffee plantations ring the city. Its churches of San Francisco and San Pedro stand out, with the Franciscan convent, schools for girls, an asylum for poor honest women, and a fine hospital. The new diocese counts about 150,000 Catholics, and Aladio Perlaza, once vicar-general of Cali, became its first bishop on 11 August 1911.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-carlo-crivell:
Carlo Crivelli was an Italian painter whose life is little known, with his birth and death reckoned from his earliest and latest signed pictures, 1468 to 1493. Possibly a pupil of Antonio and Bartolommeo Murano, he worked wholly in tempera and mastered the medium early. His pictures, sometimes stiff, are decorative and beautiful in color, lavish on single figures though weak in modern composition.

Architectural features frame his work, with lifelike fruits and flowers set in vivid relief against finely finished marbles. He labored for twenty-two years in the Marches of Ancona, especially near Ascoli, signing himself Crivellus. After knighthood from Ferdinand II of Naples in 1490, he added miles to his name. His Virgin and Child at Ascoli, dated 1493, and altarpieces in London, Berlin, and the Vatican show a painter best seen in half light at a little distance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christopher-n:
An entry on Christopher Numar of Forli, cardinal and minister general of the Friars Minor, dead at Ancona in March 1528. He studied at Bologna and Paris after joining the Friars Minor. Elected vicar provincial at Bologna in 1507 and Cismontane vicar general in 1514, and minister general of the whole order in 1517. Less than a month later Leo the Tenth made him cardinal despite his protests, praising his learning, prudence, and still greater holiness.

In 1520 Numar became Bishop of Alatri and Isernia, and in 1526 of Riez in Provence. He served with success as legate to the King of France, then as nuncio and commissary for building Saint Peter's Basilica, with temporal rule over Bertinoro. During the sack of Rome in 1527 he suffered hardships and insults. His remains were moved from Ancona to Ara Coeli in Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cosimo-rossel:
Cosimo Rosselli, a Florentine fresco painter born in 1439, earns this entry for his work in the Sistine Chapel. Four of its panels came from his hand, painted for Pope Sixtus IV. Vasari reports that their blue and gold pleased the pope above rival panels by Botticelli, Ghirlandaio, Signorelli, and Perugino.

Judged today, the panels look skilfully composed and harmonious in colour, yet weaker than their neighbours in the chapel. Rosselli's steadier claim rests on friendship with Benozzo Gozzoli and on pupils such as Fra Bartolommeo and Piero di Cosimo. Other frescoes survive in Berlin, Paris, Florence, and the National Gallery.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-daniello-bart:
A biographical entry follows Daniello Bartoli, historian and man of letters, born at Ferrara in 1608 and dead at Rome in 1685. After brilliant Jesuit schooling he entered the novitiate at Sant' Andrea in 1623, before sixteen. Tales of Jesuit labours in India and Japan fired him to seek the missions, but his general kept him in Italy.

After teaching, he preached with extraordinary success at Ferrara, Genoa, Lucca, Florence, and Rome. Concern for youth reading romances prompted his first book, The Learned Man, which ran through eight editions in its first year. Called to Rome in 1650, he wrote in Italian until his death. Best known is his six-volume history of the Society of Jesus, and his collected works filled fifty volumes at Florence in 1826.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dionigi-da-pa:
Dionigi da Palacenza Carli was one of a band of Capuchin friars sent to the Congo in 1666. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry follows the mission from Genoa through Lisbon and Brazil to Loanda and the Congo. His companion Guattini wrote an account of the voyage but died soon after landing, leaving his manuscript in Carli's hands. Carli returned to Italy a few years later, broken by sickness.

There he set down his own story of the Congo and his voyage home, rich in native manners and customs. He tells how friars died in numbers from the climate and speaks with gloom of the prospects of the mission. His book, printed in 1672 and again at Bologna in 1674, later reached English readers in Churchill's Voyages.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-evangelista-t:
Evangelista Torricelli was an Italian mathematician and physicist, born at Faenza in 1608 and dead at Florence in 1647. Schooled by the Jesuits at Faenza, he showed such skill in science that his uncle sent him to Rome in 1626. There Castelli, the favorite pupil of Galileo, taught him the master's work on motion, and his essay on the path of projectiles won Galileo's invite. Three months before Galileo's death he reached the blind scientist's house, and the Grand Duke kept him at Florence to succeed Galileo at the Academy.

His chief invention was the barometer. Tuscan pumpmakers could raise water only thirty-two feet, and Galileo fell back on nature's horror of a vacuum. Torricelli tried quicksilver, fourteen times as heavy as water, in a sealed tube set in a basin of mercury. The column fell to about twenty-eight inches, leaving the Torricellian vacuum above it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ferdinando-ug:
Ferdinando Ughelli was an Italian Cistercian ecclesiastical historian of Florence. Born in 1595, he entered the Cistercians in his native city. He became abbot of Settimo and from 1638 of Tre Fontane at Rome. Alexander VII pensioned him to fund the journeys his history required.

His Italia sacra, nine volumes from 1643 to 1662, lists the bishops of Italy in full. It holds serious errors, since Ughelli prized collecting documents over weighing them. Later scholars still consult it as a necessary foundation for critical history. He refused bishoprics and died in 1670, buried in his abbatial church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-forli:
Forli is a diocese in Romagna in central Italy, suffragan, or subordinate, to Ravenna, and its city is the ancient Forum Livii. Founded in 206 BC by the consul Livius Salinator, it was destroyed in the civil wars of Marius and Sulla, seized repeatedly by Lombards, and joined to the Papal States in 757. In the later Middle Ages the Ordelaffi family ruled it, often at odds with the popes, until Cesare Borgia seized it in 1499.

St. Mercurialis is honoured as first bishop, and the entry names later bishops, native blesseds, and churches worth seeing, including Santa Croce cathedral and San Mercuriale with its noted bell tower. The seminary held 500 Aldine first editions. At the time of writing the diocese counted 61 parishes and 60,000 people, with schools, religious houses, and a weekly Catholic paper.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fra-guglielmo:
Fra Guglielmo Agnelli, born at Pisa probably in 1238 and dead probably in 1313, was a Dominican lay brother, sculptor, and architect trained by Niccolo Pisano. Pisano had renewed sculpture on Greek and Roman models while keeping it in service to Christian art, and Agnelli joined his order at Pisa in 1257. He worked on the Dominican convent there and built the campanile, or bell tower, of the Abbey of Settimo near Florence.

His finest work is the series of marble reliefs for the tomb of St. Dominic at Bologna, made with Pisano, whose figures stand about two feet high. On the back of the tomb Agnelli carved six Dominican legends, from the healing of Reginald to Pope Honorius III approving the order's rule. The entry ranks him, for execution and importance, among the grandest Italian sculptors of his age, behind only a few names including his master.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francesco-cas:
Francesco Castracane degli Antelminelli, born at Fano on 19 July 1817 and dead at Rome on 27 March 1899. He was a priest and naturalist who became a leading student of diatoms, the tiny single-celled algae whose glassy shells fill waters and sediments. Educated at the Jesuit school at Reggio, ordained in 1840, and made a canon of Fano cathedral, he resigned his canonry in 1852. He gave the second half of his life to biological research at Rome.

He was among the first to join camera to microscope, experimenting with microphotography as early as 1862. He made diatoms his chief study, probing their structure, functions, and reproduction for what they reveal about biology, geology, and even hydrography. The great Challenger Expedition collections were entrusted to him, and among them he found three new genera, 225 new species, and some thirty new varieties. He worked to the end, saying Mass even on his last days.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francesco-deg:
Francesco Degli Angeli, also called Angelis, was a Jesuit missionary to Ethiopia, born at Sorrento in 1567 and dead at Colela in Ethiopia on 21 October 1628. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1583, spent two years in the Indies mission from 1602 to 1604, and then went to Ethiopia, the field of his life's work. Gentle and cheerful by temper, the Abyssinians called him the ever-cheerful man, and he stood high in favour with two kings in succession.

Opposition from schismatic monks blocked his great aim, reunion of the Abyssinian Church with Rome, yet he converted many, including the king's brother and lords of the court. For five years he preached among the Agazi, a half-schismatic, half-idolatrous people, winning numerous converts and founding a church and school. He translated religious works into their language, above all Maldonatus's commentary on Matthew and Luke.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francesco-del:
Francesco Della Rossa Bartholi was a Franciscan friar and chronicler of Assisi who died about 1372, known almost entirely through his own writings. He studied at Perugia in 1312 and at Cologne in 1316. Returning to Umbria with relics, including those of St. Louis of France given by the king's daughter Blanche, then a Poor Clare. He taught theology at the Porziuncula in 1320 and 1326, served as guardian at San Damiano in 1332, and was at the Sacro Convento in 1334.

Bartholi wrote several works, among them a history of the Passion. His fame rests on the Tractatus de Indulgentia Sanctae Mariae de Portiuncula, composed about 1335 and retouched through his later years. It gathers all the church documents and popular legends then available on the origin and growth of the Portiuncula Indulgence. It remains a key source for that devotion's history, first published in modern form by Paul Sabatier.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francesco-sat:
Francesco Satolli, born at Marsciano near Perugia on 21 July 1839 and dead at Rome on 8 January 1910. He was a theologian, cardinal, and the first Apostolic delegate to the United States. Educated at Perugia seminary and ordained in 1862, he taught there from 1864, served as pastor at Marsciano, and spent two years at Montecassino. He was called to Rome by Leo XIII in 1880, rising through professorships in dogmatic theology, the rectorship of the Greek College, and the archbishopric of Lepanto in 1888.

He came to America in 1889 for the centenary of the hierarchy at Baltimore and the opening of the Catholic University. On a second visit in 1892 he settled fourteen disputed school questions in New York before residing at the university as delegate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fraticelli:
Fraticelli, little friars, is the name given to various heretical sects of the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, principally in Italy, though the word is often a misnomer.

St. Francis's ideal was that his disciples, through evangelical poverty, utter self-denial, and humility, should draw the world back to Christ. Disputes over how strictly to keep that poverty tore the order apart. The Apostolics, or Pseudo-Apostles, are excluded, since their founder Segarelli was denied admission to St. Francis's order and his followers sought rather to exterminate the Minorites. The Fraticelli proper, Spiritual Franciscans driven into schism, claimed to keep Francis's rule purely while the main order compromised with property and power.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gallipoli:
Gallipoli, a diocese in Lecce in southern Italy, sits perched on a high rock above the Gulf of Taranto, joined to land by a twelve-arch bridge. Ringed by bastioned walls and a castle, it traded in wine, oil, and fish, drinking mainland water by aqueduct. Vandals wasted it in 450, and by Gregory the Great's day it belonged to the Roman Church.

Normans, Angevins, Turks, and Venetians battered it in turn. Charles of Anjou destroyed it in 1284. Venetians sacked it in 1484 and seized it in 1496, and English guns failed before it in 1809. Its proudest feat came in 1528, when 600 townsmen routed 4,000 French foot and 300 horse. Painters like Ribera, poets, jurists, and the physician Presta all called it home.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-geronimo-merc:
Geronimo Mercuriali, a philologist and physician born at Forli in 1530, revived Hippocrates for Renaissance medicine. Schooled at Bologna and degreed at Padua, he practiced at Forli, then won Rome's favor on a town errand to Paul IV, staying seven years studying classic medical writers. His On the Art of Gymnastics gathered all antiquity taught on natural cures, winning European fame.

Venetian senators called Mercuriali to Padua's medicine chair in 1569, where his Censure and Arrangement of Hippocrates' Works of 1583 led to a Greek and Latin Hippocrates at Venice in 1588. Called to Vienna in 1573 during Maximilian's illness, he pleased the emperor into making him Count Palatine. Bologna claimed him in 1587, and Tuscany's grand duke lured him to Pisa with a professor's record salary, 1,800 crowns rising to 2,000. Retiring at seventy-five to Forli, he left textbooks on children's, women's, and skin diseases widely used in medical schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giacomo-anton:
Giacomo Antonelli was the cardinal who served as Secretary of State to Pius IX and, until 1870, acted as the practical temporal ruler of Rome. Born at Sonnino in 1806, he trained in law at the Sapienza and rose through the papal diplomatic service. A Catholic Encyclopedia article traces his climb from delegate and minister to the pope's chief minister, a post he held until his death in 1876.

He became a cardinal in 1847, headed Pius's first constitutional ministry in 1848, and arranged the pope's flight to Gaeta after revolution broke out. Returning to Rome in 1850, he ran public affairs. That left the pope free to attend to spiritual duties. Admirers praised his diplomatic skill and nerve, while critics charged him with seeking personal power. The article notes he was a statesman rather than a prelate, and never became a priest.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giacomo-maria:
Giacomo Maria Airoli, also called Ayroli, was a Jesuit scholar of Eastern languages and Scripture, born at Genoa in 1660 and dead at Rome in 1721. He taught Hebrew at the Roman College and later took Cardinal Tolomei's chair of controversy. A Catholic Encyclopedia article notes his Hebrew version of a homily by Pope Clement XI as proof of his command of the language.

Sommervogel lists fourteen of his dissertations on Scripture, mostly on dates and chronology. His chief works explained notable Bible texts with Hebrew, Syriac, Chaldaic, Arabic, and Greek in 1704. They treated the seventy weeks of Daniel in 1713, and fixed the year, month, and day of Christ's death in 1718. Together the three titles show a scholar using many ancient tongues to work out questions of Bible chronology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-batt:
Giovanni Battista Casali was a musician born at Rome in 1715, who died there in 1792. From 1759 until his death he served as choir-master at St. John Lateran. A Catholic Encyclopedia article notes that his many works survive mostly in the library of Abbate Santini in Rome. He was among the last to write for unaccompanied voices.

A Mass in G major and motets such as Confitebor tibi, Ave Maria, Exaltabo, and Improperium were reprinted in Lueck's Collection at Ratisbon in 1859. Liturgical in spirit and form, they still depart from the great Roman school period in a freer use of dissonance. They also show the pull of opera, a form in which Casali himself wrote.

Giovanni Battista Riccioli was an Italian astronomer born at Ferrara in 1598, who died at Bologna in 1671. He entered the Jesuits in 1614, taught philosophy and theology at Parma and Bologna, and then gave himself wholly to astronomy. A Catholic Encyclopedia article presents a tireless worker who tried to rebuild the science on ancient and modern knowledge together.

His two-volume New Almagest of 1651, called by many the finest Jesuit literary work of the century, refuted Copernicus at length. It still praised his genius and granted his system value as a hypothesis. Riccioli's lasting gift was lunar: with Grimaldi he mapped the moon and fixed names still in use. He also measured the earth, defended the Gregorian calendar, and wrote on geography and chronology.

Giovanni Battista Scaramelli was an ascetical writer born at Rome in 1687, who died at Macerata in 1752. He entered the Jesuits in 1706, preached for fifteen years, and long served in the sacred ministry. A Catholic Encyclopedia article lists his guides for directors of souls, still reprinted long after his death.

His Directorium Asceticum of 1752 teaches, in four treatises, the means to Christian perfection and the obstacles to it. It goes on to the virtues to acquire, and to charity as the essence of perfection. His Mystical Directory of 1754 completes the method for souls led by contemplation. He also wrote on discernment of spirits and on the teaching of St. John of the Cross, in a traditional, intellectual manner opposed to Quietism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-de-m:
Giovanni de Marignolli was a Franciscan traveler born at Florence about 1290, whose place and date of death are unknown. He took the habit young at Santa Croce in Florence and later held the chair of theology at Bologna. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a mission that carried him across Asia and back over fifteen years.

Sent by Benedict XII in December 1338 to the emperor of China, he crossed Constantinople, the Crimea, and Sarai. He then crossed the Gobi desert to Peking, where he spent three years at court. He ranged through southern China, Ceylon, Java, and Sumatra, then sailed home by the Persian Gulf and the Mediterranean, reaching Naples in 1353. In 1354 the pope made him Bishop of Bisignano, and he later wrote his travels into a Chronicle of Bohemia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-meli:
Giovanni Meli was a Sicilian poet born at Palermo in 1740, who died there in 1815. Son of a goldsmith of Spanish origin, he learned first from the Jesuits, then studied science and medicine. He practiced as a physician at Cinisi and Palermo, holding the university chair of chemistry for nineteen years. A Catholic Encyclopedia article calls him unrivaled as a vernacular poet in Sicilian dialect.

Led to poetry in childhood by reading Ariosto, he found relief from domestic unhappiness in verse. His longer fantastic poems in ottava rima imitate Berni, while his Buccolica, eclogues and idylls of the four seasons, won him the name of the modern Theocritus. A staunch Bourbon supporter, he closed his work with moral fables in the manner of Aesop, carrying allegory and satire beneath the verse.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-girolamo-degl:
Girolamo degli Angeli was an eminent pioneer missionary of Japan, born at Castro-Giovanni in Sicily in 1567, who died on 4 December 1623. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1585 and began his apostolate in Japan in 1602. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a worker who stayed after the edict expelling all missionaries from the country.

Indefatigable in his labor, he was the first missionary to reach the unknown realms of Yezo, Jasu, and Cai, and made many converts to Christianity. Seeing his converts cruelly persecuted because of his presence and preaching, he gave himself up to the authorities. Condemned to death, he suffered martyrdom by fire in the public square of Yezo.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-girolamo-fran:
Girolamo Francesco Tornielli was an Italian Jesuit preacher and writer born at Cameri on 1 February 1693, who died at Bologna in 1752. He entered the Society in 1710, taught classics, then preached for almost twenty years, first at Venice in 1733, then with growing fame at Rome, Milan, Florence, and Bologna. A Catholic Encyclopedia article calls him brilliant rather than solid, and surnamed the Metastasio of the Italian pulpit.

Many hailed him as Segneri's successor, though he lacked Segneri's vehemence, impassioned logic, and directness. He had imagination and dramatic feeling, polished diction, and a refined, affecting delivery. Shocked by the licentious songs then common, he set sacred hymns to popular airs, a remedy some critics condemned. The Accademia della Crusca asked him to join and offered to publish his works, but he modestly declined.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giuseppe-agne:
Giuseppe Agnelli was chiefly known for his catechetical and devotional works, born at Naples in 1621, who died at Rome on 17 October 1706. He entered the Society of Jesus at Rome in 1637 and taught moral theology. He served as rector of the colleges of Montepulciano, Macerata, and Ancona. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a Jesuit who spent his last thirty-three years in the professed house at Rome.

His Catechismo annuale, adapted for parish priests, explained the Gospels for every Sunday of the year and went through three editions. He also wrote a week's devotion to Saint Joseph for the Bona Mors Sodality. He wrote four treatises on the Exercises of Saint Ignatius chiefly on election, a collection of meditations for a triduum and a ten-day retreat, and sermons for Lent and Advent.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gozzoli:
Benozzo Gozzoli, properly Benozzo di Lese di Sandro, was a painter born at Florence in 1420, who died at Pisa in 1497. A pupil of Fra Angelico, he assisted him at Rome and Orvieto, and began to work independently only in 1449. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a painter whose master's influence pervades work that stays personal.

His chief centres were Montefalco, Florence, San Gimignano, and Pisa, where he painted the Campo Santo's northern wall. At Florence, Piero de Medici had him fresco the palace chapel with the Procession of the Magi. The work keeps its original freshness of color and forms a portrait gallery of the Medici court. At San Gimignano he set Saint Augustine's life in seventeen frescoes, using them to picture the fifteenth-century world of learning.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heli-eli:
Two men named Heli share this entry: Eli the judge and high priest of 1 Samuel, and the Heli of Luke's genealogy. The first lived at Shiloh where the ark stood, succeeded in the judgeship by Samuel. In old age he proved weak and indulgent toward his sons Ophni and Phinehas, whose crimes brought defeat, the ark's capture, and his death at ninety-eight, falling backward and breaking his neck.

Luke calls Heli the father of Joseph while Matthew names Jacob. The entry resolves the clash through levirate law: Heli dying childless, his widow married his brother Jacob, so Joseph was Jacob's natural son and Heli's legal son. Others hold Mary herself was Jacob's daughter, making Mary and Joseph first cousins of David's house.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-januarius-mar:
One of St Alphonsus' earliest companions, Januarius Maria Sarnelli, fourth son of Baron Angelo Sarnelli of Ciorani, was born at Naples on 12 September 1702 and died on 30 June 1744. From childhood he stood out for modesty, self-denial, piety, and great diligence in studies. At fourteen he wished to become a Jesuit, but his father objected and directed him to study law, in which he succeeded admirably.

Spare time went to daily Mass, visits to the Blessed Sacrament, and care for the sick in the incurables' hospital, and at twenty-six he abandoned the bar and became a cleric. Zeal for children, whom he catechized with wonderful success, showed at once. Ordained priest in 1732, he at once joined Naples' Propaganda, a congregation of secular priests devoted to apostolic work, a lawyer turned Redemptorist pioneer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johannes-paul:
Johannes Pauli was a Franciscan preacher whose jest book, Schimpf und Ernst, holds a lasting place in German literature. Born about 1455, he took a master's degree at Strasburg, joined the Barefooted Franciscans, and preached at Thann, Oppenheim, Bern, Strasburg, Schlettstadt, and Villingen, ending his days at Thann after 1530. Little certain is known of his life, and the entry rejects the tale that he was of Jewish birth.

Prompted by knowing Geiler of Kaisersberg, Pauli published devotional books and a German version of Brant's Ship of Fools. His own masterpiece mixes farces and humorous tales with pointed satire, written in an easy style meant to instruct while it amused. Drawing on many sources, his stories inspired later German poets, above all Hans Sachs, and shaped the culture of the whole century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-franz-:
Joseph Franz Allioli was a German Bible scholar and translator who lived from 1793 to 1873. Born at Sulzbach, he studied theology at Landshut and took ordination at Ratisbon in 1816, and learned Eastern languages at Vienna, Rome, and Paris. He taught at Landshut and Munich, then took a canonry at Ratisbon and became dean at Augsburg in 1838.

Allioli wrote on Hebrew antiquities and biblical geography and, with Grätz and Haneberg, produced a handbook of biblical antiquities. His chief work was a German translation of the Old and New Testaments from the Vulgate, in six volumes from 1830 to 1835, which received papal approval in 1830.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-leonardo-anto:
Leonardo Antonelli (1730-1811) was a cardinal and diplomat, born at Sinigaglia. Early on he served as Secretary of the Sacred College, Assessor of the Holy Office, canon of the Vatican Basilica, and keeper of archives in San Angelo's Castle. Pius VI made him Cardinal-Priest of St. Sabina in 1775, and he later became Dean of the College.

At the French Revolution he backed the vote for the French clergy's civil constitution, decreed 12 July 1790. He also served as grand penitentiary and prefect of the Signature of Justice and the Congregation of the Index. He helped prepare the Concordat, attended Pius VII's election in 1800, and went with him to Paris in 1804. Banished by the French in 1808 to Spoleto and then Sinigaglia, he died leaving bequests to Propaganda for twelve Armenian students at the College of Urbano. He owned a rich library and won some fame as an archaeologist.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-libellatici-l:
The libelli were certificates issued to third-century Christians. Certificates of conformity attested that holders had met the religious tests of Decius's edict. Certificates of indulgence carried the intercession of confessors or martyrs for the lapsi, those who had apostatized. The scornful term libellatici applies only to holders of the first kind. Decius's edict of 249 or 250, after a long peace, frightened many Christians into submission.

Submission took several forms: apostates who left the faith, sacrificati and thurificati who joined pagan rites, and libellatici who bought conformity certificates. Three such libelli survive, all Egyptian, in which the petitioner claims constancy in sacrificing and begs commissioners to sign. Sometimes the declaration stood for the deed, or the paper was bought. For reconciling lapsi, confessors sent libelli pacis to the bishop, asking their own merits to win remission of temporal punishment, believed to avail before God.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-luca-signorel:
Luca Signorelli was an Italian painter, born at Cortona about 1441 and dead there in 1523. Son of Egidio, nephew by marriage to Vasari's kin, he trained under Piero della Francesca and felt Pollaiuolo's pull, painting in a Florentine mode.

High office at Cortona, burgher rank at Citta di Castello, and a judge's seat for Florence cathedral's facade marked his civic life. At Monte Oliveto in 1497 he painted eight frescoes, then spent five years at Orvieto on the Last Judgment, his most personal work, with a bold self-portrait. Rome work for Julius II vanished for Raphael's, yet he painted at Cortona almost to his death at eighty-two.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lucas-pacioli:
Lucas Pacioli was an Italian mathematician, born at Borgo San Sepolcro toward the mid-fifteenth century and dead probably soon after 1509. Little is known of his life beyond his Franciscan habit and his teaching at Perugia, Rome, Naples, Pisa, and Venice.

At Milan he shared the court of Ludovico Sforza with Leonardo da Vinci until the French invasion. His Summa of 1494, drawing freely on Fibonacci, preserved lost fragments of that earlier master and became the base for Cardano and Tartaglia. His Divine Proportion of 1509, with Leonardo's help, treated polyhedra and the use of letters for numbers, and his Euclid followed the same year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-luigi-ferdina:
Luigi Ferdinando, Count de Marsigli, was an Italian geographer and naturalist, born at Bologna in 1658 and dead there in 1730. Of an old patrician house, he added mathematics, anatomy, and natural history to a gentleman's schooling, and learned by watching the world himself.

Venice sent him to Constantinople in 1679 to report Turkish forces and the Bosporus, and Leopold's service in Hungary saw him wounded and enslaved in 1683, then ransomed in 1684. He later fixed Venetian, Turkish, and imperial borders, but Breisach's surrender in 1703 broke his sword and honours, though opinion later cleared him. Home at Bologna, he gave his whole collection to the Senate in 1712.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-melozzo-da-fo:
Melozzo da Forli, an Italian painter of the Umbrian school born at Forli in 1438, died there in 1494. Lanzi's guess that he studied under Ansuino da Forli rests on nothing solid. Little is known of Ansuino beyond a small share in the Eremitani Chapel frescoes at Padua, finished before 1460. Through him Melozzo might have learned from Mantegna, but more likely he felt no influence except Piero della Francesca's.

Piero, ever absorbed in perspective and author of a treatise on it, gave Melozzo his mastery of the subject. He also gave him a love of large tableaux and the heroic cast of his work. Melozzo was among the artists Federigo da Montefeltro summoned to Urbino's court, perhaps introduced by Giovanni Santi, Raphael's father. None of his Urbino work survives, though the Barberini Palace in Rome holds part of the series, including pictures from the duke's study of 1476.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-monopoli:
Monopoli is a diocese in the province of Bari, Apulia, whose town holds a small but good harbour on the Adriatic and succeeded the ancient Egnatia, whose ruins lie nearby. Saracens ravaged it through the eighth and ninth centuries, and after the Norman counts arrived it became the seat of Hugues in 1042.

Its bishopric dates to 1062 under its first prelate, Deodatus, and the second bishop, Romualdus, raised the cathedral in 1073. Polignano joined the diocese in 1118, and during the French-Spanish wars for Naples the Venetians seized and sacked the town twice, in 1495 and 1528. Charles V ringed it with walls and towers in 1552 that still stand, and the diocese, directly subject to Rome, counts eight parishes and 65,000 people.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nephtali:
Nephtali, sixth son of Jacob and Bilhah, bears a name explained by a wordplay that perplexes commentators. Modern interpreters, following Simonis and Gesenius, render it wrestlings of God have I wrestled with my sister, and I have prevailed, making Nephtali mean my wrestling, or simply wrestling. Pseudo-Jonathan says Nephtali first told Jacob that Joseph lived, and counts him among the five Joseph presented to Pharaoh.

The apocryphal Testament of the Twelve Patriarchs says he died in his 132nd year and was buried in Egypt, but those details are unreliable. Certainty extends only to his four sons: Jahzeel, Guni, Jezer and Shillem. His tribe counted 53,400 warriors at the first census, sixth among Israel's tribes, and 45,400 at the second, eighth. The entry follows the tribe through the desert wanderings, settlement, and later history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-niccolo-anton:
Niccolo Antonio Zingarelli, composer, was born at Naples on 4 April 1752 and died at Torre del Greco on 5 May 1837. Trained at the Loreto Conservatory under Fenaroli and Speranza, his first opera Montesuma played at San Carlo on 13 August 1781. He stayed in Milan until 1794, then served as maestro di cappella at Loreto's Santa Casa until 1804, succeeding Guglielmi as Sistine Chapel choir master.

For refusing to conduct a Te Deum for Napoleon in Saint Peter's in 1811, he was taken prisoner to Paris but soon released. In 1816 he replaced Paisiello as Naples cathedral choir master until death. Deeply religious, he devoted most attention to masses, oratorios, cantatas and motets, composing 541 works for Loreto including 28 masses. His Giulietta e Romeo of 1796 counts as his best opera, and his requiem, written for his own funeral, shows his most devoted church style.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicola-giacom:
Camaldolese monk Nicola Giacomo Mittarelli, known in religion as Gian Benedetto, wrote the history of his own order from Venice. Born in 1707, he joined the Camaldolese at fourteen, taught philosophy and theology, and rose to abbot of San Michele di Murano and then general of the order.

His nine-volume Annals of the Camaldolese, published from 1755 to 1773, follows Mabillon's model for the Benedictines and runs from 907 to 1770. Shorter histories of monasteries at Treviso and Faenza round out a life spent in archives and teaching. His posthumous catalogue of Saint Michael’s manuscripts appeared at Venice in 1779.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolo-machia:
Florentine statesman Nicolo Machiavelli, born in 1469, watched power at close range for fourteen years as secretary of the republic. He ran its home and foreign correspondence, kept council minutes, drafted treaties, and went on twenty-three embassies to France, the emperor, Rome, and Cesare Borgia.

Dismissed when the Medici returned in 1512, Machiavelli turned to writing, and his Prince and Discourses on Livy drew hard lessons from history about holding states. The entry weighs his sharp observation against charges of cynicism, and he died at Florence in 1527. His family had given Florence thirteen gonfaloniers of justice, though his father was far from wealthy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolo-maria-: Nicolo Maria Antonelli, a cardinal, canonist, historian, and scholar of the East born at Sinigaglia in 1698, defended the parish character of Rome's ancient churches in a 1725 treatise. He also edited and backed Athanasius on the Psalms. He put out sermons of James of Nisibis in Armenian and Latin and issued a Lateran missal for monks under a borrowed name before his death in 1767.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paolo-dal-poz:
Paolo dal Pozzo Toscanelli was a Florentine mathematician, astronomer, and cosmographer, born in 1397 and dead at Florence on 10 May 1482. Son of the physician Dominic Toscanelli, he began mathematics under Giovanni dell'Abacco, then entered Padua at eighteen to study mathematics, philosophy, and medicine. There he formed a lifelong friendship with Nicholas of Cusa.

Both left Padua in 1424, Nicholas as doctor of canon law and Paolo as doctor of medicine, whence his nickname Paolo the physician. Back at Florence for life, save short trips in Tuscany, Todi, and Rome, he became a centre of learned Europe. Regiomontanus and Cusa sought his counsel on the hardest questions, and his letters, maps, and gnomon work shaped the age's geography and astronomy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-petrus-aureol:
Peter Aureoli was a Franciscan philosopher and theologian called the Eloquent Doctor, born at Toulouse about 1280. He joined the Friars Minor, taught theology at Toulouse and Paris, became provincial of Aquitaine in 1319, and was named Archbishop of Aix by John XXII in 1321, dying the next January. Eloquence earned his title, and his pen defended the Immaculate Conception.

He argued the doctrine in a public debate at Toulouse in 1314, in his De Conceptione Mariae Virginis and its Repercussorium, in sermons, and in comments on St. Bernard. His works on the Sentences, his Quodlibeta, and his scriptural handbook saw many editions. In philosophy he was a conceptualist before Occam, criticizing Aquinas and partly siding with Scotus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pietro-castel:
Pietro Castelli was an Italian physician and botanist who laid out Messina's botanical garden and wrote on an extraordinary scale. He was born at Rome in 1574 and studied under Andrea Cesalpino. He taught at Rome from 1597 to 1634, then moved to Messina, where in 1635 he planted a garden of exotic medicinal herbs.

He insisted that every physician study anatomy, claiming by 1648 to have dissected more than a hundred bodies. He published some hundred and fifty pamphlets. One of 1653, answering a Genoese inquiry, is the first Italian publication to mention cinchona, the Peruvian bark used against malaria, though Castelli himself knew little of the plant or its use.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pietro-france:
Pietro Francesco Mazzuchelli, known as Il Morazzone, was a Milanese painter born at Morazzone near Milan in 1571 or 1575, who died at Piacenza in 1626. Early in life he lived in Rome, painting altarpieces, then moved to Venice. There he studied Titian, Tintoretto, and Paolo Veronese so deeply that his later Milan pictures, on similar subjects, could hardly be recognised as from the same hand.

Cardinal Borromeo patronised him, and the Duke of Savoy knighted him with the order of Saint Maurice. In 1626 he was called to Piacenza to paint the cathedral cupola, begun in a grand and vigorous style. He died, it is believed, from an accident on the scaffolding, and Guercino was called to finish the work. His chief painting, Saint Michael and the angels, stands in San Giovanni at Como.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pozzuoli:
Pozzuoli, in the province of Naples on its gulf, was built by the Cumaeans as their port, under the name Dicaearchia. Carthage used it in the Second Punic War. Rome took it, walled it, and named it Puteoli. Hannibal tried in vain to take it. Made a Roman colony in 194 BC, it grew into Italy's chief port, with rare town freedoms.

Alaric besieged and sacked it in 410, Totila in 545, and Grimoaldo II of Benevento in 715. Naples took it in 1014, and it passed with Naples to the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies. Quakes shook it in 1448 and 1538, and Turks landed in 1550. Ruins of villas and shrines still speak of its old splendour. Chief is the Temple of Serapis, shrine and bath house in one. Digs in 1838 bared an amphitheatre for 30,000 and hot baths. Paul landed here on his road to Rome and met brothers, as Acts tells.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-de-nob:
Robert de Nobili was a Jesuit missionary who sought to convert India's Brahmins by living as one of them. Born at Montepulciano in Tuscany in 1577, he entered the Society of Jesus in 1597 and sailed for India in 1604, reaching Goa in May 1605. Sent to Madura in 1606 to study Tamil, he mastered Tamil, Telugu, and Sanskrit within a year.

To reach the Brahmins he adopted their way of life, cutting himself off from fellow missionaries. He worked in Madura, Mysore, and the Karnatic until age and near blindness forced his retirement to Mylapore. He translated or composed many prayers and works in Sanskrit, most lost during his imprisonment at Madura in 1639-41. His chief Tamil work, the Larger Catechism in four books, adapts theology to Indian needs. He also enriched Tamil and Telugu with fitting Christian terms. He died at Mylapore in 1656.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rorate-coeli:
Rorate Coeli are the opening words of Isaiah 45:8 in the Vulgate. The text is used often at Mass and in the Divine Office during Advent, voicing the longings of patriarchs, prophets, and the Church for the coming of the Messiah. Throughout Advent it occurs daily as versicle and response at Vespers. The verse divides into a versicle asking heaven to rain down justice and a response asking earth to bring forth a Saviour.

The text also serves as Introit for the Fourth Sunday in Advent, for Wednesday in Ember Week, and for the feast of the Expectation of the Blessed Virgin. It also serves votive Masses of the Virgin during Advent. It appears as versicle, antiphon, and responsory in various Advent offices, including Lauds and Matins before Christmas. Its plain-song Introit appears in the Vatican Graduale and the Solesmes Liber Usualis of 1908.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rotuli:
Rotuli, or rolls, were long narrow strips of papyrus or parchment, written on one side and wound about a staff like a blind. They formed the earliest kind of volume. Many such rolls survive in primitive form from Herculaneum and elsewhere. In the fourth and fifth centuries rolls gave place to bound books, leaves laid flat and attached by their edges.

For certain purposes rolls were still kept, including legal records, manuscripts for chanting the Exultet, and mortuary rolls. A mortuary roll bore at its head the notice of a death, then travelled by special messenger from monastery to monastery, each house entering receipt and promising suffrages. Entries often grew into complimentary verse of many lines. Flourishing most in the eleventh, twelfth, and thirteenth centuries, these rolls preserve ornate verse valuable for palaeography and for judging scholarship across learning centres.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ruggiero-giov:
Ruggiero Giovanelli was a composer, born at Velletri near Rome in 1560 and died at Rome on 7 January 1625. In 1584 he became choir-master at San Luigi de' Francesi in Rome, and later at the Chiesa dell'Anima. As a madrigal composer he was exceedingly fertile: six books of madrigals, with one of canzonets and vilanelles, appeared between 1585 and 1606.

So great was his fame as choir-master and composer that on Palestrina's death he was appointed his successor on 12 March 1594. Among his sacred works are beautiful masses for eight and twelve voices and pleasing motets. So little was known of his later years that biographers once found no trace of him after 1615, when he published the second volume of his new Medicean Graduale. Research by W.H. Frey of Berlin proved he lived ten years longer. He was buried in Santa Marta.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sandro-bottic:
Sandro Botticelli, the famous Florentine painter, was born at Florence about 1447 and died there in 1510. Properly Alessandro di Mariano Filipepi, he took his name from the painter and goldsmith Botticelli, his first master. Later he studied under Fra Filippo Lippi, learning the ideal manner of Fra Angelico. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia explains a style and a conversion.

Through Verrocchio and the Pollaiuolo brothers, that idealism joined the naturalism of Masaccio, a blend that shaped later painters. Botticelli lived quietly and modestly, working for the Medici and other great Florentine houses from about 1483 to 1500. Worldly by temper, he was shaken by Savonarola's call to repentance, which turned his art, it seems, into new paths, though he never learned to manage money.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-savona-and-no:
Savona and Noli form a diocese in Genoa province on the Gulf of Genoa, with a small but safe harbour. Besides sea trade and shipbuilding, the people make steel, glass, delft, and majolica, and quarry lignite and marble. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia tours churches and palaces before its history.

The cathedral, dating from 1589 and restored in the nineteenth century, has three naves and a cupola with fine Coghetti frescoes. Beside it stands the Sistine chapel built by Sixtus IV, whose family came from Savona. The Rovere palace, built by Sangallo, lost Semini's paintings when turned into a convent. Once called Sabbatia, Savona's bishops were its counts in the tenth century, before the countship passed to Monferrato and then Vasto under Genoa's shadow.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-scalimoli:
Scalimoli, a theologian better known by his religious name Andrea di Castellana, came from Castellana in Apulia. He joined the Conventual Franciscans in the St Nicholas province of Bari and later served as its provincial. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia centres on one handbook for workers among Protestants. The book is short and plain in aim.

He laboured in Moldavia, Wallachia, and Transylvania, served Hungary as prefect apostolic, and inspected Franciscan missions in Russia as visitor general. That experience taught him what such a guide must hold. The order's general approved the work in 1642, and it was dedicated to Cardinal Barberini. His 1644 Bologna volume tells a missionary, trained by Propaganda, how to live among heretics and refute their errors. It shows how to grow in the faith across Germany, Poland, and Hungary, wherever Lutheran teaching flourished.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-soli:
Soli was an ancient port city on the south-western coast of Cyprus, and this entry follows it from its founding legends to its place in the early Church. Said to have begun as an Athenian colony under the name Oepea, it moved to a better site at the prompting of Solon, whose name it took. And became the capital of one of the island's nine kingdoms, with temples to Aphrodite and Isis.

Its later history is thin, though ancient geographers mention it often, and its ruins lie near the village of Karavostasi. The entry also names its first bishop, St. Auxibius, said to have been baptized by John Mark. And two later bishops whose feasts the Greek Church still keeps, making it a useful stop for readers tracing Cyprus in antiquity and early Christianity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ambrose-of:
St. Ambrose of Camaldoli, born Ambrose Traversari at Portico near Florence on 16 September 1386 and dead on 21 October 1439, was an Italian theologian and writer of rare linguistic gifts. Entering the Camaldolese order at fourteen and becoming its general in 1431, he knew Greek as well as Latin, and those gifts drew him into the highest church affairs.

Eugenius IV sent him to the Council of Basle, where he defended the primacy of the Roman pontiff and begged the council not to tear Christ's seamless robe. He then went to Emperor Sigismond to seek aid against a council trenching on papal rights for five years. When the pope moved the council to Ferrara in 1437, Ambrose's efforts and charity toward poor Greek bishops greatly helped the cause of union at Ferrara and Florence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-eusebius-o:
Eusebius of Vercelli, bishop from 340 to 371, joined monastic life to parish clergy in the West for the first time. Born in Sardinia about 283, he served as lector in Rome, then was unanimously elected at Vercelli and consecrated by Pope Julius I on 15 December 340. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Vercelli to 1 August 371.

Ambrose testifies that Eusebius led his city clergy in a common life modelled on Eastern cenobites, which is why Augustinian canons honour him as a founder beside Augustine. In 364 Liberius sent him with Bishop Lucifer to Constantius at Arles, seeking a council for the faith. The entry presents a bishop whose household of clergy became a model for Western monastic clergy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stefano-anton:
Stefano Antonio Morcelli, an Italian Jesuit and epigraphist, mastered ancient inscriptions and classical Latin. Born at Chiari near Brescia on 17 January 1737, he studied at Brescia's Jesuit college and entered the Society on 3 November 1753. He taught grammar at Fermo, humanities at Ragusa, and oratory at the Roman College, founding an archaeology academy at the Kircher Museum.

After the Society's suppression in 1773 he became librarian to Cardinal Albani, and in 1791 took a provostship in his native town. He declined the archbishopric of Ragusa and died a member of the restored Society on 1 January 1822. His fame rests on vast knowledge of inscriptions and on classical Latinity. Chief works include De stilo inscriptionum latinarum of 1781, Inscriptiones of 1783, a Constantinopolitan calendar of 1788, and Africa Christiana of 1816 to 1817.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-syncelli:
Syncelli were monks or clerics who shared a room with their bishop in the early Church. The name joins syn, with, to kellion, a Greek form of Latin cella, cell. Their duty was to witness the purity of the bishop's life and to share his daily spiritual exercises. In the Eastern Church they soon grew into councillors and confessors of patriarchs and bishops, wielding great influence.

They ranked first after their masters, holding a seat and vote in church councils. In time patriarchs took two or more syncelli, the chief being called protosyncellus. Their power waned after the tenth century, though they still exist in the Greek Church. In the Latin Church they never grew so strong, but gradually became papal and episcopal spiritual councillors.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-takkali:
The Takkali, more properly Takhehi, are the Carrier Indians of British Columbia's northern interior. Fur traders named them, sometimes sweeping in the Chilcotin and Babine peoples too. Carriers proper live in permanent villages from Lake Tatla to Alexandria. Speech splits them into Lower and Upper branches, divided between Stuart and Fraser Lakes. They number some 1,614 people in twelve villages.

Missionary care has lately raised several villages. Their southern neighbours the Chilcotin fared worse, falling from 1,500 in 1864 to about 450. Babines, once 2,000 strong around their lake, now number barely 430 with their Bulkley kin. Carriers and Babines follow matriarchy. Titles and property pass through women. Hereditary petty chiefs alone own clan hunting lands.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-termoli:
Termoli stands on Italy's Adriatic coast, with a small harbour near the Petraglione's mouth. Anciently called Buca, it was put to fire and sword by Turks in 1567. It holds a fine Gothic cathedral. It first appears as a diocese in 946, when the usurper Benefetto was forced out by order of Agapitus II. Its earliest known legitimate bishop was Scio in 969. Successors include Jacopo Cini, a Dominican author of a commentary on the Sentences in 1379, and Domencio Girada, a learned Servite theologian in 1381.

Federico Merzio, bishop in 1602, collaborated with Baronius. In 1818 the see united with Guardia Alferia, a small town near Cerrato whose bishops ran from 1075 to 1775. Termoli is suffragan of Benevento and holds 19 parishes, 54 secular priests, and one convent of nuns.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tivoli:
Tivoli is a diocese in the Province of Rome, set where the Anio River drops nearly three hundred feet from the Sabine hills into the Roman Campagna. Its falls draw many visitors, and their water power runs local industries and lights Rome. Olive groves, vineyards and gardens cover the nearby slopes, and paper making is the chief local trade.

The great cascade dates only from 1835, when the Gregorian tunnel through Monte Catillo gave the river a safe outlet. Ruins of temples to Hercules and Tiburtus overlook the falls, and Hadrian's vast villa, covering 173 acres with theatre, baths and library, lies nearby. The diocese, subject directly to the Holy See, counted forty-two parishes, forty thousand people, and sixty-nine secular and thirty-five regular priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ucayali:
San Francisco de Ucayali was a prefecture apostolic in eastern Peru's mountainous forest region, La Montaña. A prefecture apostolic is a mission district below a diocese in rank. At the Peruvian government's request, the Holy See erected three prefectures there on 5 February 1900, hoping the Indian tribes of that secluded country would be civilized and converted. All three answered directly to the Propaganda in Rome. The central one, Ucayali, stayed in Franciscan hands.

The entry maps the prefecture's three districts. One covers the country drained by the Perene and Pachitea with the Gran Pajonal. The Apurimac country runs along the Ene, Mantaro, and Tambo rivers, and the third district reaches toward the upper Ucayali itself. It names the mission stations and the friars at work among peoples reached only by river and forest trail.
